Jaundice arises from a disruption in the normal metabolism and excretion of bilirubin, a byproduct of hemoglobin breakdown from senescent red blood cells (RBCs). This can lead to an increase in unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin, which then leaks back into the bloodstream, leading to jaundice . Neonatal jaundice is a particularly common condition, affecting approximately 60% of term and 80% of preterm newborns in their first week of life
Symptoms: Yellow skin/eyes, dark clay-colored stools, intense itching from bile salts, right upper abdominal pain, nausea.
Causes: Jaundice can be caused by a wide variety of causes, including pre-hepatitis, viral hepatitis, cirrhositis, hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E, as well as genetic disorders of bilirubin metabolism.
Preventions: Vaccines can prevent viral hepatitis, a common cause of hepatic jaundice. Safe medication use can help prevent non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, a growing cause of liver damage.
Treatment: Jaundice is a medical condition characterized by bilirubin deficiency.
When to See a Doctor: Any visible yellowing:** If skin, eyes or mucous membranes appear yellowish, especially if accompanied by other symptoms. This is particularly important for adults, as jaundice often indicates significant underlying disease.
